Today we study the business world.
We will look at economic systems, the public sector and the main economic indicators.
Then we will focus on two topics: the green economy and youth unemployment.
After each topic you will find a short review and a quiz. Let's start!
S1: An economic system answers three questions: what to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce.
In a free-market economy, the market forces of supply and demand decide, and private companies are the main actors.
In a command, or planned, economy, the government controls everything and establishes the prices.
The mixed economy is the most common system in the modern world: the government controls essential services like health and education, and the private sector follows supply and demand.
S2: The public sector is the part of the economy controlled by the state. It is paid for with money from taxes.
At the end of the twentieth century, many governments started to privatise public corporations. Privatisation is a controversial phenomenon.
In the last two decades, public ownership has come back at a local level. This is called remunicipalisation.
The advantages: essential services are protected, there is no duplication of services, prices are lower and stable, and profits go back to the government.
The disadvantages: more bureaucracy, slow decisions, political influence, lack of competition, and losses paid for by the state through taxes.
S3: GDP, Gross Domestic Product, is the total value of goods and services produced within the borders of a nation in a year.
GNP, Gross National Product, is the GDP plus money earned from investments abroad, minus money earned by non-citizens and foreign businesses within the nation.
The business cycle has four phases: expansion, recession, depression and recovery.
Inflation is the increase in prices. Most economists favour a low and steady rate, around two per cent, and central banks control it with interest rates.
With deflation, prices fall, and economic development slows down. Shrinkflation is a form of hidden inflation: the product gets smaller, but the price stays the same.
A healthy economy has low unemployment, between three and five per cent. Governments can reduce it with retraining, incentives for businesses and lower taxes.
S4: Natural capital is nature's contribution to the economy: water, air and land.
The green economy improves human well-being in the long run, without exposing future generations to environmental risks.
To achieve sustainable growth, natural capital and the green economy must become part of economic decision making.
Today consumers look for sustainable products, so companies should adapt to this change in consumption trends.
S5: The NEET rate measures the percentage of young people, aged fifteen to twenty-four, who are Neither in Employment nor in Education or Training.
In twenty twenty, twenty-two point four per cent of young people were NEET, and most of them were girls and young women.
There is a gender gap: the NEET status is more permanent for girls, mainly because of family responsibilities.
